slides.body: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery.
In video 170 the workflow involved two servers.
Chapter 27 reduces the subject to one sentence: a branching strategy is nothing but an agreement about which refs exist, who may move them, and in which direction commits travel between them.

We go through five things: branch names, GitHub Flow, Git Flow with a replayed history, the 2020 note, and then GitLab Flow, trunk-based development, release branches and Microsoft's Release Flow, each as a graph.
Here's what you'll walk away with.

slides.headline: Step 1: the release branch
slides.body: 🟡 CAUTION: git merge moves the current branch.

lines.s: git merge --no-ff -m "Merge release/1.4.0 back into develop" release/1.4.0
# Features were merged into develop, not main. A release branch stabilizes them:
# The release branch is merged back so that develop has the version bump too:
git merge --no-ff -m "Merge release/1.4.0 back into develop" release/1.4.0

slides.headline: Step 2: the hotfix
slides.body: It starts from main, which is what production runs, not from develop.

git commit -q -am "Fix limit 0 being treated as unlimited"
git merge --no-ff -m "Merge hotfix/1.4.1 into develop" hotfix/1.4.1

slides.body: Five mistakes to watch for.

items: Treating a branch name as a control. Root cause: Git gives no meaning to a name; only a platform setting, a ruleset pattern or automation that triggers on the pattern gives it force.

Adopting Git Flow for a continuously deployed service. Root cause: the model was conceived for explicitly versioned software with several supported versions, and a service with one live version has nothing for develop and release branches to separate.

Calling GitHub Flow and trunk-based development opposites. Root cause: both have one long-lived branch; the difference is a limit on branch lifetime and, in the strictest form, the pre-merge review gate.
Forgetting the merge back in Git Flow. Root cause: a release or hotfix lives on two long-lived branches, and the model needs a second merge to carry it to develop; nothing in Git reminds you.
Naming a release branch inconsistently. Root cause: rules and deployment workflows select branches by pattern, so a branch outside the pattern is outside the rule.

slides.body: Let's land this, in your own words.

items: A branch name means nothing to Git; a default-branch setting, a ruleset pattern or a workflow filter gives it force.
GitHub Flow is one always-deployable branch with short branches and deployment after merge, and it assumes one live version.

Git Flow is main plus develop plus feature, release and hotfix branches with merges in two directions; its author restricted it in 2020 to explicitly versioned software with several supported versions.
Trunk-based development limits branch lifetime to a couple of days; release branches are cut late from the trunk, receive only fixes and are never merged back.
The question that sorts the models is how many versions are alive at once.

beats.text: Branch names are conventions, not laws. main, develop, feature/*, bugfix/*, hotfix/* and release/* are names that people agreed on. Git gives none of them a meaning.
beats.tele: Branch names are conventions, not laws. `main`, `develop`, `feature/*`, `bugfix/*`, `hotfix/*` and `release/*` are names that people agreed on. Git gives none of them a meaning.

beats.text: To Git, refs/heads/release/1.4 is a ref whose name happens to contain a slash. The slash matters in exactly two technical ways. It lets patterns select groups of branches: git branch --list 'release/*', a ruleset target such as release/**, a workflow filter such as branches: ['release/**']. And in the files backend it makes release a directory, so a branch named release and a branch named release/1.4 can't both exist.
beats.tele: To Git, `refs/heads/release/1.4` is a ref whose name happens to contain a slash. The slash matters in exactly two technical ways. It lets patterns select groups of branches: `git branch --list 'release/*'`, a ruleset target such as `release/**`, a workflow filter such as `branches: ['release/**']`. And in the files backend it makes `release` a directory, so a branch named `release` and a branch named `release/1.4` can't both exist.

beats.text: GitHub Flow. One long-lived branch that is always deployable, short branches off it, a pull request for each, and deployment right after the merge. Deployable means that it can go into service for users at any moment, and a pull request is GitHub's object for proposing and reviewing a merge.

beats.text: GitHub's documentation describes six steps: create a branch, make changes, create a pull request, address review comments, merge, delete the branch. Scott Chacon's 2011 essay, where the name comes from, adds the rules that give it its character: anything on the main branch is deployable, and you deploy immediately after merging.

beats.text: He also gives the reason GitHub didn't use Git Flow: GitHub deployed many times a day, while Git Flow is organised around releases. Martin Fowler's reading is that the model assumes a single production version, so release branches and hotfix branches disappear: a hotfix is one more short branch.

beats.text: What it assumes: that there is one live version, that main can be deployed at any commit, and that a broken deployment is repaired by rolling forward or back quickly. Microsoft's description of its own practice records where the strict form stops scaling: when a repository completes more than 200 pull requests a day, deploying each one before or after merge turns into a queue, so Microsoft batches deployments into sprint releases instead.

beats.text: Git Flow. Two long-lived branches, main for released code and develop for integration, plus three kinds of supporting branch: feature, release and hotfix.
beats.tele: Git Flow. Two long-lived branches, `main` for released code and `develop` for integration, plus three kinds of supporting branch: feature, release and hotfix.

beats.text: Vincent Driessen published "A successful Git branching model" on the fifth of January 2010. Feature branches start from and merge into develop, with --no-ff so that each feature stays visible as a unit. A release branch is cut from develop, receives only stabilization commits, and is merged into main, and tagged, and back into develop. A hotfix branch is cut from main, and is merged into main, and tagged, and into develop.

A release branch is cut from `develop`, receives only stabilization commits, and is merged into `main`, and tagged, and back into `develop`. A hotfix branch is cut from `main`, and is merged into `main`, and tagged, and into `develop`.

beats.text: GitLab Flow. GitLab defines it as a simplified strategy that works directly with main and adds, where needed, a production branch, environment branches such as staging and production, or release branches for software shipped in versions. Three of its eleven published rules: fix bugs in main first and release branches second, base releases on tags, and never rebase pushed commits.

beats.text: Trunk-based development. Developers integrate into one branch, the trunk, and avoid other long-lived development branches. Very small teams may commit straight to the trunk. Larger teams use short-lived feature branches, which should last no more than a couple of days, belong to one developer or a pair, and be deleted after the merge.

Larger teams use short-lived feature branches, which should last no more than a couple of days, belong to one developer or a pair, and be deleted after the merge.

beats.text: Long-running changes are handled with feature flags and a technique called branch by abstraction, instead of long branches. A feature flag is a condition in the code that keeps unfinished behavior switched off. Fowler treats it as close to a synonym for continuous integration.

beats.text: The difference from GitHub Flow is one of degree, not of kind. Both have one long-lived branch. Trunk-based development adds a limit on branch lifetime and, in its strictest form, drops the pre-merge review gate.

beats.text: Release branches. A release branch is cut from the trunk shortly before a release, receives only fixes, and is the place the release and its patches are tagged. The trunk-based development site states the rules: cut late. The branch may start from a commit older than the trunk's head.

beats.text: It's never merged back. It's deleted when the version is no longer supported. And bugs are reproduced and fixed on the trunk first and cherry-picked to the release branch. A cherry-pick copies one commit's change onto another branch as a new commit with a new ID.

beats.text: Microsoft's Release Flow. Short-lived topic branches are merged to main through pull requests with branch policies. At the end of each three-week sprint a release branch is created, named for the sprint. The document's example is releases/M129. It's deployed in rings. A hotfix is made in main first and then cherry-picked to the release branch through its own pull request.

beats.text: Now one question that sorts them all. All of these models keep one integration branch. They differ in what, if anything, sits downstream of it, and in which direction a fix travels.

beats.text: Use this as the sorting question: how many versions are alive at once? If the answer is one, there's nothing downstream of main, and you're somewhere between GitHub Flow and trunk-based development. beats.text: A branch name means nothing to Git; a default-branch setting, a ruleset pattern or a workflow filter gives it force.
beats.tele: A branch name means nothing to Git; a default-branch setting, a ruleset pattern or a workflow filter gives it force.

beats.text: GitHub Flow is one always-deployable branch with short branches and deployment after merge, and it assumes one live version.
beats.tele: GitHub Flow is one always-deployable branch with short branches and deployment after merge, and it assumes one live version.

beats.text: Git Flow is main plus develop plus feature, release and hotfix branches with merges in two directions; its author restricted it in 2020 to explicitly versioned software with several supported versions.
beats.tele: Git Flow is `main` plus `develop` plus feature, release and hotfix branches with merges in two directions; its author restricted it in 2020 to explicitly versioned software with several supported versions.

beats.text: Trunk-based development limits branch lifetime to a couple of days; release branches are cut late from the trunk, receive only fixes and are never merged back.
beats.tele: Trunk-based development limits branch lifetime to a couple of days; release branches are cut late from the trunk, receive only fixes and are never merged back.

beats.text: The question that sorts the models is how many versions are alive at once.
beats.tele: The question that sorts the models is how many versions are alive at once.

beats.text: Read sections 27.5 to 27.8. Then read git help workflows, the Git project's own workflow document, which the chapter cites. Note what it says about the branch on which a fix is committed. You'll need that sentence in the next video, where one release and one hotfix are run under two strategies.
